author: bridge-bot
content:
<stkux> Maybe I have to jump in at this point. As interesting and good light clients are, for most applications, a light client is not feasibility as it needs too much resources. That's the reason why RPC services are that successful - but they are not trustless.

What we really need for mass adoption is stateless clients, which do not sync nor store state information nor be part of an p2p network. What is needed is trustless data which is information and proofs which can be executed and validated in the client. 

This we have done with colibri.stateless and the future should be vRPC (verifiable RPC - data plus proof). So, RPCs are data providers, but not trusted anymore.

author: bridge-bot
content:
<stkux> For Apps, this means: using a stateless client like colibri.stateless is as easy and doesn't consume more resources. Data is verified on protocol level, privacy (read privacy with PAP) can be added on protocol level. And the whole client starts with about 250kB. 

And the other good thing: to replace the trusted RPC connection with the colibri.stateless client is not much more than 2 or 3 lines of code. No additional syncing or anything like this. No additional protocol is needed, no new infrastructure is needed.

The proofs can be created locally, or more efficiently served trustless by a prover service, or even more efficient, RPC providers start serving also vRPC (data + proofs together)

author: bridge-bot
content:
<stkux> To use the SNAP protocol to read data is still an interesting idea, but if this would be successful used in many dApps, we would have the same issues as with LES some years before. Why should nodes serve those clients as they do not reward any benefit to the network. Other than with ancient LES, there is also no reward layer included in SNAP (as far as I know).
If SNAP is heavyly used as source of data, it most probably will not be available for these clients (like LES). 

Nevertheless, to use this mechanism as fallback in a stateless client, if no RPC is available as data provider, could be quite interesting. Then you have a good security net for the hopefully very unlikely event that no RPC service is reachable.

author: bridge-bot
content: <b1afra> The problem with LES was that it was off by default. So there was never a chance that enough clients would have it enabled.

author: bridge-bot
content: <b1afra> Even if you can verify RPC data in a client, that doesn't make RPC providers permissionless nor censorship proof. And you're still leaking everything to one entity.

author: dirkjaeckel
content: Isn't the idea of a Merkle tree that you don't need the full tree? You only need the root hash and the path to the value you want to verify.

author: sky.cactus
content: You need the root hash plus the hash of every sibling along your path.

author: sky.cactus
content: Which is why merkle proofs are generally considered pretty heavy weight.

author: bridge-bot
content:
<stkux> re: **@b1afra**
> Even if you can verify RPC data in a client, that doesn't make RPC providers permissionless nor censorship proof. And you're still leaking everything to one entity.
This is not fully correct. First, colibri.stateless supports multiple RPC or decentralized RPC networks. That means, one RPC can't censor. 

Regarding privacy: to realize read privacy, you can run your own client (or a p2p light client), or you use privacy mechanisms to not leak your intend and/or identity. In colibri.stateless, we implemented PAP (Pragmatic adaptive privacy), our privacy model on protocol level. Depending on the demands, different privacy levels can be used.
